questions.q: Why can the phrase 'data governance' itself work against a program when talking to a business audience?
options: "Data" reads as a tactical IT concern and "governance" reads as bureaucracy, risking a tuned-out audience before the substance lands
The phrase is trademarked and cannot be used outside of IT
Business audiences are generally unfamiliar with the word "data"
Executives require a different term for legal reasons
questions.explain: The lesson identifies this as a real word problem — the term itself can trigger a dismissive reaction before any real content is communicated.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend having ready before any other communication about governance?
options: One plain-language, jargon-free sentence defining data governance without acronyms or framework names
A full slide deck covering every chapter of the governance program
A signed executive memo distributed to all staff
A glossary of all metadata and lineage terminology
questions.explain: The lesson gives a specific one-sentence definition — rules, roles, and responsibilities for how data is created, stored, accessed, and used — with no jargon, as the starting point for any audience.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'constraint framing' and 'enabler framing' of the same governance policy?
options: Constraint framing leads with the restriction ("you can't..."); enabler framing leads with what the policy makes possible ("here's the faster way to...")
Constraint framing is used for executives, enabler framing is used for frontline staff
Enabler framing only applies to pilot programs, not full roadmaps
The two framings describe different, unrelated policies
questions.explain: The lesson gives paired examples showing the same underlying policy described as a restriction versus described as what it enables — the content is identical, but reception differs sharply.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what role does the executive sponsor typically play in a manager-only briefing channel?
options: Equipping managers to answer their own teams' questions, rather than delivering the message directly to frontline staff
The sponsor delivers the exact same all-staff speech to managers
The sponsor has no role in manager briefings
The sponsor replaces the data stewards in that channel
questions.explain: The channel table in this lesson distinguishes sponsor roles by channel — manager briefings are about equipping people leaders, while office hours are mostly steward-led and one-on-ones are where the sponsor spends political capital directly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a real pilot result is more persuasive than a framework slide when communicating governance?
options: It is a specific, measurable, concrete outcome rather than an abstraction like "better data culture"
Framework slides are not allowed in business communications
Pilot results are always larger in scale than what a framework could show
A pilot result requires no executive sponsorship to share
questions.explain: Communication grounded in something concrete that actually happened — like reconciliation time cut from Lesson 27's pilot — outperforms communication that relies on abstract claims.
